sources.entry: Nuitka - Compiles Python programs into high-performance standalone executables (cross-platform).

summary.one_liner: Nuitka is a Python compiler written in Python that translates Python programs and modules into C and builds them into standalone executables, extension modules, or packages.
summary.what_it_does: Nuitka compiles Python 2.6/2.7 and Python 3.4–3.14 code to C, which is then built with a C compiler and runs alongside libpython, per the README. It can produce a standalone folder (--mode=standalone), a single file (--mode=onefile), a compiled extension module (--mode=module), or a compiled package (--mode=package). Users can follow imports recursively, include data files and package data, and add Windows or macOS icons, version info, and macOS app bundles. It also supports multidist, which bundles several entry-point programs into one binary with shared modules, and setuptools/pyproject integration for building wheels. The README also describes a compilation report and a custom report template option.
use_cases: Compile a Python program into a standalone executable
Distribute a Python app to machines without Python installed
Build a Python package or module as a compiled extension (.so/.pyd)
Bundle several Python programs into one binary
Build wheels with setuptools or pyproject.toml using Nuitka
Automate Python binary builds in GitHub workflows
notable: Compiles Python constructs into C that runs with CPython, keeping compatibility with uncompiled code and libraries
Standalone and onefile modes make binaries runnable without a Python install
Multidist mode combines several programs into one binary, choosing the entry point from sys.argv[0]
Supports Nuitka-Action for GitHub workflows and in-code nuitka-project options
caveats: Requires a C compiler (C11 or C++03), with platform-specific choices; MinGW64 does not work with Python 3.13 or higher
Must run on CPython, Anaconda, or Homebrew Python; Windows Store Python and macOS pyenv are stated not to work
Data files are not automatically handled in all cases; the README says users are largely on their own with them
Some features such as file embedding and certain options are only in the commercial edition
